name: Third-party cookies by browser (Nov 2026)
plain: Whether an embedded site can set and read its own cookies on other sites, which varies by browser.
meaning: Third-party cookies are how ad networks recognise the same person across sites. Safari blocks them, Firefox partitions them, Brave blocks them, Chrome leaves them on by default (user choice) and blocks them in Incognito.

web.api: document.cookie in iframes; Set-Cookie with SameSite=None; Secure; Storage Access API

access.persistence: Cookie lifetime per cookie; Chrome caps at 400 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

chrome.note: 3PC allowed by default; blocked in Incognito

samsung.note: Allowed by default, Smart Anti-Tracking blocks some

data.metric: Cookie jar per top-level site (partitioned) or global

limits.headline: Can recognise you across sites with embedded cookies, unless your browser blocks them
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page with ads or embeds loads
can: Set and later see its own cookie from inside a page on another site
Link your visits across the sites that embed it
Keep working in Chrome, where these cookies stay on by default
Ask the browser for access if it was blocked (Storage Access prompt)
cannot: Set these cookies in Safari, which blocks them
Share one cookie across sites in Firefox, which keeps a separate jar per site
Use them in Incognito windows in Chrome
Get through in Brave, which blocks them
limits.differs: Safari and Brave block them, Firefox splits them per site, and Chrome allows them by default but blocks them in Incognito.

story.what_it_is: Whether an embedded site can store cookies on other sites, which depends on which browser you use.

marketing.name: Intelligent Tracking Prevention
marketing.pitch: Safari blocks cross-site tracking by default so websites cannot follow you from site to site.

marketing.name: Enhanced Tracking Protection
marketing.pitch: Firefox keeps each site's cookies in a separate jar so trackers cannot connect your visits.

marketing.name: Privacy Sandbox
marketing.pitch: Chrome kept third-party cookies and gives people a choice, while offering newer ad tools as alternatives.

story.for_you: You never see these cookies, but they decide whether an ad for boots follows you from a shoe shop to a news site. In Safari and Firefox it mostly cannot. In Chrome it still can, unless you turn it off in settings.
story.for_makers: Ad networks use these cookies to recognise the same person across sites for targeting, frequency caps and conversion counting. Sites also use them for legitimate embeds like logins and payments. When a browser blocks them, makers must switch to first-party data or new APIs.

use_cases.example: A retailer's ad network sets a cookie when you view boots, then recognises you on a recipe blog and shows the same boots.
A Like or Share button embedded on a news article recognises your logged-in account and counts the visit.
An embedded video on a blog remembers your player settings and view history through the video host's own cookie.
A browser game embedded in a portal page saves your progress under the game host's cookie, which breaks when the browser blocks it.
A card check inside a frame on a shop page relies on the bank's cookie to recognise a trusted device.
A bot defence service sets one cookie across many customer sites to spot a scraper hopping between them.
A marketing platform ties an ad click on one site to a purchase on another to report which campaign worked.

risks: Settings differ by browser, so protection is uneven

technical_bounds: Safari: blocked for all, no exceptions except Storage Access API
Firefox: Total Cookie Protection partitions per top-level site by default (June 2022, Firefox 103)
Chrome: kept on by default; no deprecation prompt after the April 2025 decision; Incognito blocks by default
Edge: Tracking Prevention blocks classified trackers, not all

legit_uses: Embedded video, chat, SSO, payment frames
abuse: Cross-site profile building by ad networks

history.change: Total Cookie Protection default for all users
1% of Chrome users had third-party cookies restricted (testing)
Google proposed user choice instead of deprecation
